title: Algorithms
overview: A2 algorithms brings together searching, sorting, ADTs and efficiency. You need to write/trace linear search, binary search, insertion sort and bubble sort; manipulate stacks, queues, linked lists and binary trees; explain graphs and dictionaries; and compare time/space complexity using Big O.
syllabusPoints: Write/trace linear and binary search and state the precondition for binary search.
Write/trace insertion and bubble sort and analyse how input order/size affect performance.
Find, insert and delete items in specified ADTs such as stacks, queues, linked lists and binary trees.
Explain graphs/dictionaries and how ADTs may be implemented from built-in types or other ADTs.
Compare algorithms using time and space efficiency and Big O notation.

definitions.definition: A notation describing how time or memory requirements grow as input size n grows.
A tree ordered by key so smaller values are placed in one subtree and larger values in the other.
An ADT storing key-value pairs accessed by unique keys.
LIFO structure: last item added is first removed.
FIFO structure: first item added is first removed.

sections.title: Linear and binary search
content: Linear search checks items one by one and works on unsorted data; worst-case time grows O(n). Binary search repeatedly halves a SORTED range; worst case O(log n). The cost of initially sorting data may matter if only one search will ever be done.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: Binary search: compare target with middle; discard one half; repeat until found or interval empty.

sections.title: Bubble sort
content: Compare adjacent items and swap out-of-order pairs. After each pass an extreme element moves to its final end position. A swap flag can stop early if a pass makes no swaps. Worst-case behaviour is quadratic.

sections.title: Insertion sort
content: Maintain a sorted prefix. Take the next value, shift larger values right, and insert it into the correct location. It can be efficient on small/nearly sorted input but worst case is also O(n^2).

sections.title: Stacks and queues
content: Array implementations need indices/pointers plus overflow/underflow tests. Stacks push/pop at the top. Queues enqueue at the rear and dequeue at the front; circular queues reuse freed array positions without shifting every item.

sections.title: Linked lists
content: Each node contains data plus link(s). Search follows links. Insert/delete often change only a few links once the position is known, avoiding array shifts, but traversal is usually sequential because nodes are not indexed by position.

sections.title: Binary trees
content: Search compares a key and descends left/right. Insertion descends until a free child location. Performance depends on shape: a balanced tree can be efficient, while a severely skewed tree behaves much more like a list.

sections.title: Graphs and dictionaries
content: Graphs model arbitrary many-to-many relationships such as transport/social networks. Dictionaries map keys to values and can be implemented using hashing or tree structures. Choose implementation according to lookup, insertion, ordering and memory requirements.

sections.title: Big O and trade-offs
content: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n^2) quadratic. Big O describes growth, not exact seconds. Space complexity matters too: a faster algorithm can require more memory.

examTips: Binary search requires sorted data—state this every time you justify it.
For ADT pseudocode include empty/full/null checks where relevant.
Use Big O for scaling and then add practical context such as preprocessing or memory.
commonMistakes: Assuming every binary search tree is balanced.
Forgetting to update head/root pointers during insertion/deletion.
Comparing algorithms only by execution time when the question asks for efficiency criteria.
